documentation:
## Neural Network

### What it does
This graph uses a trained neural network to solve the inverse kinematics a 3-axis mechanical rig. When a user sets the intended end effector position of the rig using the `ik_CTRL` in the Maya scene, the neural network predicts the necessary rotation values for the rig to reach that position and sets them on the bifrost rig accordingly.

### Inputs and outputs 

The main inputs to the graph are:
- The `data_directory` on the `data_inputs` compound, which should be set to the directory that holds the trained neural network weights. A directory of pretrained weights have been included with this example; however, should you can change the directory to point to your own model weights, should you choose to retrain the model on your own rig
- The `ik_LOC` transform takes the user input from the graph, specifying the desired end effector location of the rig. This is conceptually the same as an IK Handle on a conventional rig.
- The `root_LOC` transform allows the user to specify the base frame of the rig in which the IK solve happens. You can parent this control in Maya to another object that you want to transform, like a vehicle chassis.
- An array of `pivot_locators`, which represent the pivot points of each axis in the rig's rest pose. These transforms can be modified by moving the associated `locator*` in the Maya scene, but these locations must correspond to the rig topology that was used to generate the training dataset.
- You can optionally input an array of `meshes` to represent the rig geometry. 

The output of the graph is the vizualization of the rig in Maya's viewport in the proper configuration given the user input

### Useful information

This example is intended to be paired with the `generate_data` example graph to show an end-to-end machine learning pipeline where data is procedurally generated, a neural network is trained on that data, and then the trained neural network is deployed to accomplish the intended task. 

In this case, we are approximating an inverse kinematic (IK) solver on a 3-axis mechanical rig. Each axis consists of a revolute joint that rotates about a single axis. 
Please see the `generate_data` example for more information on generating the data and training the neural network.

The result of the training is a network that can be given a new end effector position `[x, y, z]` and it will predict the joint rotation values `[theta_1, theta_2, theta_3]` required for the rig to reach that position, effectively performing an IK solve.
While this example shows an IK solve, the fundamental workflow is applicapable to many such problems where data can be generated procedurally in the graph, and then the trained network can be deployed back in the graph to accomplish a specific task.

The `compute_ik_cascade` compound shows how the neural network building blocks can be composed to perform the layer computations of a neural network given the trained model parameters. Upon inspection, you'll notice that this particular network is a four layer neural network with ReLU activation functions.

The `compute_ik_loop` > `iterate_over_layers` compound shows this same network as done in an iterate loop
